title: Nagle and delayed ACK
text: A small order can sit in your own kernel for tens of milliseconds, waiting for an acknowledgement that is itself waiting. Here is how two sensible rules collide.

title: Nagle's algorithm
text: In 1984, John Nagle described the small packet problem. One typed character went out as a 41 byte packet: 1 byte of data, 40 bytes of headers. His fix: while any sent data is still unacknowledged, hold new small writes back. They go out together when the ACK arrives, or once a full-sized segment has built up. On the busy networks of 1984, that overhead was a real problem.

title: Delayed ACK
text: Receivers save packets too. RFC 1122 lets a TCP delay its ACK, so it sends fewer of them. The delay must stay under half a second, and in a stream of full-sized segments, at least every second one gets an ACK. On Linux, the delayed ACK timer runs between 40 and 200 milliseconds. Fewer ACKs means less work for both ends.

title: The collision
text: Now put them together. Your gateway writes order one, and it goes out at once. Order two follows a moment later, but order one is unacknowledged, so Nagle holds it. The other side has nothing to send back yet, so it delays its ACK. Order two waits for that timer: tens of milliseconds, for a message that should take microseconds. Nothing is broken and nothing is lost: both sides are following the rules.

title: TCP_NODELAY
text: The fix is one socket option. TCP_NODELAY turns Nagle off for that connection, and RFC 1122 says every TCP must offer a way to do that. Segments then go out as soon as possible, even small ones. Linux also has TCP_QUICKACK for the receiving side, but the man page warns it is not permanent: the kernel can return to delayed ACKs.

title: In the lab
text: The lab's TcpStream sets TCP_NODELAY in its constructor, so every accepted or connected order socket has it. Sends never block. Whatever the kernel cannot take at once goes into a queue, and flush drains it later. So if bytes are waiting, they wait in the lab's own queue, where the program can see them, not inside the kernel.

title: The flip side
text: With Nagle off, every write becomes its own packet. Write a header and a body in two calls, and you send two segments, each with 40 bytes of headers or more. So build the whole message, or a whole batch, in one buffer, and write it once. One write per message also means one system call per message, not two.

title: Takeaway
text: Nagle saves bandwidth by waiting. On an order path, turn it off, and write whole messages. Next: what happens when a packet reaches the card, and who notices.
